vedic_reference.note: Asmita is a term used in Hinduism and Buddhism to denote the individual self or ego. It is derived from the Sanskrit word ātma (आत्मा), which means 'self' or 'soul'.

historical_references.reference: Asmita is believed to be an incarnation of Goddess Parvati, the wife of Lord Shiva. According to Hindu mythology, Asmita was born as the consort of Lord Indra, the king of gods. Indra, in the guise of a sage, had married Asmita, but she later revealed her true identity and abandoned him. Out of jealousy, Indra attempted to kill Asmita with his thunderbolt. To protect Asmita, Lord Shiva intervened and absorbed her into his body. From then on, Asmita is considered to be an aspect of Lord Shiva.

In Jainism, Asmita is considered as one of the five great Tattvas or elements, representing the individual soul or ego. In Jain scriptures, Asmita is described as the soul which cannot be destroyed and which is always pure and conscious. It is believed that the ultimate goal of Jainism is to liberate the soul from Asmita or ego, leading to Moksha or salvation.
